prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

I remember the first day, how I looked down, hoping you wouldn't see me, and when I glanced up, I saw your smile shining like a soft light from deep inside you. “I'm listening,” you encourage us. “Come on! Join our conversation, let us hear your neon certainties, thorny doubts, tangled angers,” but for weeks I hid inside. I read and reread your notes praising my writing, and you whispered, “We need you and your stories and questions that like a fresh path will take us to new vistas.” Slowly, your faith grew into my courage and for you— instead of handing you a note or apple or flowers— I raised my hand. I carry your smile and faith inside like I carry my dog's face, my sister's laugh, creamy melodies, the softness of sunrise, steady blessings of stars, autumn smell of gingerbread, the security of a sweater on a chilly day.

prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Come, Join, Slowly

outputs.L1:
I remember the first day: how I looked down, hoping you would not see me, and how, when I finally glanced up, I saw your smile shining like a soft light from deep within you.

“I’m listening,” you encouraged us. “Come on—join our conversation. Let us hear your neon certainties, your thorny doubts, your tangled angers.” Yet for weeks, I stayed hidden inside myself. I read and reread your notes praising my writing, and you seemed to whisper, “We need you—your stories and questions that, like a fresh path, will lead us to new vistas.”

Slowly, your faith grew into my courage. And for you—instead of handing you a note, an apple, or flowers—I raised my hand.

I carry your smile and your faith within me, just as I carry my dog’s face, my sister’s laugh, creamy melodies, the softness of sunrise, the steady blessings of stars, the autumn scent of gingerbread, and the security of a sweater on a chilly day.
outputs.L2: I can still picture that opening day: my eyes fixed downward, wishing to stay unnoticed. Then I lifted my gaze and found you smiling, a gentle brightness seeming to glow from within. “I’m listening,” you would tell us, urging us on. “Please—enter the discussion. Share your bright convictions, your sharp uncertainties, your knotted frustrations.” Still, for many weeks, I stayed hidden within myself. I studied your comments again and again, the ones that praised my writing, and you quietly told me, “We need you—your stories, your questions—the kind that open a new trail and lead us toward places we haven’t seen before.” Little by little, your belief in me became my own bravery, and for you—not with a note, an apple, or a bouquet—I lifted my hand. I keep your smile and your confidence in me close, the way I hold my dog’s face in memory, my sister’s laughter, smooth music, the tender hush of daybreak, the constant gifts of the stars, the gingerbread scent of fall, and the comfort of a warm sweater in cold weather.
outputs.L3:
At first, the speaker was shy and preferred to remain unnoticed in the classroom. They often stayed quiet, hoping not to attract attention or be asked to speak in front of others. The classroom felt like a place where they could listen silently, but not a place where they felt brave enough to share their own ideas.

However, the teacher created an atmosphere of warmth and encouragement. She invited everyone to take part in the lessons by sharing their thoughts, asking questions, expressing doubts, and telling their own stories. Her classroom was not just a place for studying; it was a space where every voice mattered.

Over time, the teacher began to notice the speaker’s writing and praised it with genuine belief. Her kind words made the speaker feel seen and valued. She believed in the speaker’s ability, and that belief slowly helped the speaker develop confidence. The praise was not just encouragement; it became a source of strength.

Eventually, the speaker found the courage to raise their hand and join the classroom conversation. This was an important moment because it showed how much they had grown. What once felt frightening became possible because of the teacher’s support and faith.

Even now, the speaker continues to cherish the memory of the teacher’s smile and her belief in them. Her encouragement remains a lasting source of comfort and strength, reminding the speaker that their voice matters and that confidence can grow when someone truly believes in you.
outputs.L4:
I used to be the quietest student in the classroom.

Every morning, I would take my seat near the back, lower my eyes, and hope the teacher would not call on me. I listened carefully to every lesson. I knew many of the answers. Sometimes the words would form clearly in my mind, and I would feel a sudden urge to say them aloud. But the moment I imagined everyone turning to look at me, my courage disappeared. My heart would beat fast, my hands would grow cold, and I would stare down at my notebook as if the answer were hidden there.

Speaking in class seemed simple for other students. They raised their hands without hesitation. They asked questions, made mistakes, laughed, and tried again. I admired them, but I could not be like them. I was afraid of saying the wrong thing. I was afraid my voice would shake. Most of all, I was afraid that people would laugh.

My teacher noticed.

She never forced me to speak before I was ready. Instead, she encouraged me in small, quiet ways. When she walked past my desk and saw that I had written the correct answer, she would smile and say, “Well done.” When I completed an assignment carefully, she would write a kind comment at the bottom of the page. Sometimes, after class, she would say, “You have good ideas. I hope one day you will share them with everyone.”

At first, I did not believe her. I thought she was only being kind because teachers were supposed to be kind. But she kept saying it. She kept noticing my efforts. She praised me not only when I was right, but also when I tried. Slowly, her words began to stay with me.

One day, during a lesson, she asked a question. I knew the answer immediately. As usual, I looked down and waited for someone else to speak. But this time, no one raised a hand. The room was silent.

My teacher’s eyes moved around the classroom and then rested gently on me. She did not call my name. She did not put pressure on me. She simply smiled, as if to remind me that she believed I could do it.

I felt my heart begin to race. My fingers trembled under the desk. For a moment, I almost gave up. Then I remembered all the times she had told me that my ideas mattered. I remembered the praise written on my papers, the patient smiles, and the quiet encouragement that had followed me day after day.

Slowly, I raised my hand.

It was such a small movement, but to me it felt enormous. My arm seemed heavy, and my face grew warm. The teacher called on me in the same calm voice she used with everyone else.

I gave my answer.

My voice was soft at first, but the words came out clearly enough. The class listened. No one laughed. When I finished, my teacher’s face lit up with pride.

“That’s exactly right,” she said. “Thank you for sharing.”

Those few words filled me with a feeling I had never known before. I felt seen, not because I had been perfect, but because I had been brave. From that day on, raising my hand became a little easier. I still felt nervous sometimes, but the fear no longer controlled me. Each time I spoke, my confidence grew.

My teacher’s faith in me changed the way I saw myself. She taught me that courage does not always appear suddenly. Sometimes it grows slowly, through patience, kindness, and someone believing in you before you are able to believe in yourself.

Even now, when I feel afraid to speak or try something new, I remember her encouragement. I remember the day I raised my hand for the first time. Her belief became a lasting source of courage, comfort, and self-confidence—something I carry with me wherever I go.
outputs.L5:
Come, take a step closer and leave the noise behind. There is no need to rush, no need to have everything figured out at once. Sometimes the best journeys begin quietly, with one small decision and one gentle breath.

Join the path that leads toward new moments, new people, and new possibilities. Walk with an open heart, and let each experience teach you something simple but meaningful. Together, even the longest road feels lighter.

Slowly, we learn to notice the beauty around us—the warmth of a smile, the comfort of friendship, the strength found in patience. Slowly, we grow. Slowly, we become who we are meant to be.

So come, join the journey, and move forward slowly. The destination will arrive in its own time.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poetic thank-you letter from a shy student to a teacher who helped them find the courage to speak in class, using vivid sensory imagery and a warm, reflective tone.
counterfactuals.output:
Dear Teacher,

I used to keep my words folded small inside me,  
like notes tucked at the bottom of a desk,  
creased from being held too long.

In class, voices rose around me like sunlight through tall windows—  
bright, easy, golden—  
while mine stayed quiet as dust on a windowsill.  
I knew the answers sometimes.  
I felt them flutter in my chest,  
soft as a bird beating its wings behind my ribs,  
but fear would close my throat like a winter door.

You never forced it open.

Instead, you waited with the patience of warm tea cooling in a cup.  
You smiled in a way that said, *Take your time.*  
You listened even when I only managed a whisper,  
and somehow my whisper did not feel small in your classroom.  
It felt like the first green shoot pushing through dark soil.

Because of you, I learned that a voice does not need to be loud  
to be brave.

I still remember the day I raised my hand.  
My palm was damp.  
My heartbeat sounded like rain against the roof.  
The room seemed too bright, the air too thin—  
but your eyes were kind and steady,  
like a lamp left on to guide someone home.  
When I spoke, my words trembled,  
but they stood.

And you let them stand.

Thank you for hearing the courage inside my quiet.  
Thank you for showing me that mistakes are not storms to hide from,  
but puddles to step through.  
Thank you for making the classroom feel less like a stage  
and more like a garden,  
where even the shyest voices could bloom.

I am still learning to speak,  
but now, when my words rise,  
I do not always swallow them back.  
Sometimes I let them enter the air—  
small, bright, and real.

With deep gratitude,

Your student
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a lyrical first-person prose piece about remembering a supportive teacher’s smile and encouragement, ending with a list of comforting things the narrator carries in their heart.
counterfactuals.output:
I still remember my teacher’s smile.

Not the way one remembers a fact written on a chalkboard, but the way one remembers sunlight falling across a cold room—sudden, gentle, and impossible to forget. It arrived before her words did, softening the air around me, telling me I was not as small as I felt.

There were days when my hands trembled over my notebook, when every answer seemed to hide behind a locked door, when I believed mistakes were proof that I did not belong. She would pause beside my desk, bend close enough for me to hear the quiet steadiness in her voice, and say, “Try again. You’re closer than you think.”

Those words stayed with me.

They followed me through hallways loud with other people’s confidence. They sat beside me during exams, during failures, during long evenings when the world felt too heavy to lift. Her encouragement became a small lantern inside me. Whenever doubt gathered like fog, I could see her smile there, patient and bright, reminding me that learning was not a race away from weakness, but a brave return to the page.

I understand now that she gave me more than lessons. She gave me a way to look at myself with kindness. She showed me that a voice can become shelter, that belief can be lent to someone until they grow their own, that a single moment of gentleness can echo for years.

And so, even now, I carry her with me—not as a memory that fades, but as a warmth I return to.

In my heart, I carry:

- her smile, steady as morning light  
- her words: “You’re closer than you think”  
- the courage to begin again  
- the patience to learn slowly  
- the kindness she taught me to offer myself  
- the quiet belief that I am still growing  
- the comfort of knowing someone once saw my possibility and called it by name
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a short free-verse style tribute to an English teacher, mentioning class discussions, praised writing, hidden doubts, and the student finally raising their hand.
counterfactuals.output:
For the English teacher—

who turned class discussions  
into open windows,  
who found bright edges  
in our uneven sentences  
and praised the writing  
we were almost afraid to claim.

You never saw, perhaps,  
the hidden doubts  
folded beneath my notebook cover,  
the questions I kept quiet  
like pressed leaves.

But your voice made room  
for mine.

And one day,  
with my heart loud as a bell,  
I finally raised my hand.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Rewrite the idea “my teacher believed in me and helped me share my voice” as an emotional, image-rich paragraph with metaphors involving light, paths, stars, autumn, and warmth.
counterfactuals.output: My teacher was the first warm light to find me in the quiet corners where I had hidden my voice. When I felt like a path covered in autumn leaves, uncertain and easy to lose, they walked beside me, gently clearing the way with patience and belief. Their words were small lanterns in my hands, teaching me that even my softest thoughts could glow. Under their care, I began to see my voice not as something fragile, but as a star waiting for the courage of night to shine. In the warmth of their faith, I learned to step forward, speak honestly, and leave my own light on the path for others to follow.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft a heartfelt appreciation passage for a teacher from the perspective of a quiet student, including quoted encouragement like “I’m listening” and imagery such as neon certainties, thorny doubts, and tangled angers.
counterfactuals.output:
As one of the quiet students in your class, I may not always raise my hand or find the right words out loud, but I want you to know how deeply I appreciate you.

You have a way of noticing people even when they don’t ask to be seen. On days when my mind was full of thorny doubts, when my thoughts felt heavy and my confidence felt small, you never rushed me or made me feel invisible. Instead, you offered steady encouragement, the kind that stays long after the lesson ends. Sometimes it was as simple as, “I’m listening,” but those words meant more than you may realize. They made the classroom feel safe. They reminded me that my voice mattered, even when it came quietly.

In a world that can feel confusing, you gave us neon certainties—bright reminders that effort counts, kindness matters, and learning is not about being perfect, but about continuing. You helped me sort through tangled angers, fears, and frustrations without making me feel ashamed of having them. You taught with patience, but also with heart.

Thank you for believing in me in the moments when I was still learning how to believe in myself. Thank you for hearing the students who speak softly, for seeing the ones who sit silently, and for making your classroom a place where even quiet growth is celebrated. Your kindness has made a lasting difference, and I will carry it with me.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
